title: The 8-Phase Workflow: How dotai Turned AI Coding Agents Into Spec-Driven Engineers
author: Niaz Bin Siraj
excerpt: AI coding agents are powerful but undisciplined. dotai v3.0.0 introduces Spec-Driven Development, an 8-phase workflow that transforms agents from unpredictable code generators into accountable engineers who implement exactly what you specified.
contents:
AI coding agents have a fundamental problem. They are remarkably good at generating code from natural language prompts, but without guardrails they tend to hallucinate scope, invent features that were never requested, and produce output that technically runs yet misses the original intent entirely. The root cause is not a lack of intelligence. It is a lack of structure.

With dotai v3.0.0, I set out to solve this by introducing Spec-Driven Development (SDD), a structured 8-phase workflow that forces AI agents to follow a specification at every step, with human review checkpoints and automated evaluation. The result is a development process where agents implement precisely what was agreed upon and can prove it.

Why Conversational AI Coding Breaks Down

Most developers interact with AI agents the same way: describe what you want, let the agent write code, review it, find problems, go back and forth correcting, and eventually ship something that is close enough. For small, isolated tasks this works reasonably well. But for anything substantial, a feature spanning a dozen tasks across multiple files with interconnected logic, the conversational approach collapses under its own weight.

The agent has no persistent memory of agreements. There are no formal acceptance criteria. There is no mechanism for the agent to verify its own work against a standard. Every correction cycle adds latency and risks introducing new misalignments. The core issue is that natural language is ambiguous, and ambiguity compounds across a long implementation.

What if there were a specification artifact at every step, reviewed by a human and enforced by automated evaluation? That is the premise behind the 8-phase workflow.

The Two Halves: Specification and Execution

The workflow splits cleanly into two halves. Phases 1 through 4 handle specification, where the intent is captured, formalized, decomposed, and planned. Phases 5 through 8 handle execution, where code is written, evaluated, reviewed, and the knowledge base is updated. No code is written until the specification is locked down and reviewed.

Phase 1: Initiate   - idea.md (you write this)
Phase 2: Specify    - requirements.md (AI generates, you review)
Phase 3: Decompose  - task files (AI generates, you review)
Phase 4: Plan       - plan + evaluation files (AI generates, you review)
Phase 5: Implement  - source code (AI executes)
Phase 6: Evaluate   - PASS/FAIL per task (AI verifies, loops on failure)
Phase 7: Review     - code-review.md (AI + you)
Phase 8: Sync       - knowledge/ updated (AI)

Four human review checkpoints. Zero wasted implementation cycles on misunderstood requirements.

Phase-by-Phase Walkthrough

Phase 1: Initiate (Human Only)

You create a new feature directory and write an idea.md file. There is no enforced format here, just raw intent. Describe what you want to build, why it matters, and any constraints you already know about. This document is the single source of truth that everything downstream traces back to.

dotai sdd new user-authentication

The command scaffolds the feature directory. You fill in the idea. Everything else flows from this file.

Phase 2: Specify (AI Agent)

The Requirements Agent reads your idea.md and produces a structured requirements.md that covers functional requirements, user flows, edge cases, and non-functional constraints. The critical rule enforced here is that the agent does not invent scope. It only formalizes what you already implied or stated.

/sdd-specify user-authentication

Human Review Checkpoint. This is arguably the most critical review in the entire flow. A misaligned requirements document will silently corrupt every downstream phase. Catch misunderstandings here, not after implementation.

Phase 3: Decompose (AI Agent)

The Decomposer Agent breaks the approved requirements into discrete, ordered tasks. Each task is scoped small enough for a coding agent to execute independently without making assumptions. The output is a set of numbered task files like 01_project_setup.task.md and 02_data_model.task.md.

/sdd-decompose user-authentication

Human Review Checkpoint. Task order and granularity directly control how implementation unfolds. If a task is too broad, the coding agent will fill in gaps with assumptions. If tasks are too granular, coordination overhead increases. Finding the right balance is critical.

Phase 4: Plan (AI Agent)

For each task, the Planner Agent produces two outputs: a plan file describing exactly how to implement the task, and an evaluation file defining the acceptance criteria. The evaluation file is what Phase 6 will enforce, so this is where you define what "done" means for every single task, before any code exists.

/sdd-plan user-authentication

Human Review Checkpoint (final gate before code). Once you approve the plans and evaluation criteria, the specification is locked. The coding agent now has an unambiguous contract to fulfill.

Phase 5: Implement (Coding Agent)

The coding agent works through the task list in order, one task at a time. For each task, it reads the .task.md and .plan.md files and implements accordingly. There is no room for creative interpretation or scope expansion. The plan defines the boundaries.

/sdd-implement user-authentication

Phase 6: Evaluate (Evaluator Agent)

This is where Spec-Driven Development earns its keep. For each completed task, the Evaluator Agent reads the .evaluation.md file and checks the implementation against every acceptance criterion. It produces a .result.md with a PASS or FAIL verdict and detailed findings.

/sdd-evaluate user-authentication

If any task fails, the loop returns to Phase 5. The coding agent receives the failure details and reattempts only the failing task. No code advances past Phase 6 until every criterion is satisfied. The status reporting gives you visibility into progress at any point:

Phase 5: Implement    - 7/12 tasks implemented
Phase 6: Evaluate     - 7/12 tasks evaluated (6 passed, 1 failed)

Phase 7: Review (AI + Human)

Once all tasks pass evaluation, the Code Review Agent reads the entire codebase holistically. Rather than reviewing task by task, it examines the system as a whole, looking for issues only visible at scale: inconsistent patterns, redundant logic, missed optimizations, and security concerns.

/sdd-review user-authentication

Human Review Checkpoint (final gate). You read the review report and decide what must be addressed before shipping.

Phase 8: Context-Sync (AI Agent)

The Context Agent updates the project's .ai/knowledge/ directory, refreshing memory files, documenting patterns and gotchas, and updating codebase documentation to reflect everything built and decided during this feature cycle. The next development session starts with full awareness of what exists.

/sdd-sync user-authentication

Three Principles That Make It Work

1. Specification Before Implementation

Every line of code traces back to an approved spec. The agent does not interpret a vague prompt. It follows a plan that you already reviewed and corrected. This eliminates the single biggest source of waste in AI-assisted coding: implementing the wrong thing.

2. Evaluation as a First-Class Concept

Acceptance criteria are not an afterthought. They are written before implementation begins and enforced automatically after implementation completes. Failures trigger automated retries, not manual debugging sessions. The evaluation loop is the mechanism that guarantees the specification is actually honored.

3. Human Gates at Critical Moments

The workflow does not remove humans from the loop. It positions them at the four most impactful review points: after requirements, after decomposition, after planning, and after the final code review. Every review happens before the downstream work begins, preventing wasted effort on misaligned foundations.

Cross-Tool Compatibility

Because dotai manages a single .ai/ directory as the source of truth and symlinks it to every supported tool's configuration, SDD commands work identically across Claude Code, Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, and Antigravity. The 28 command files are generated automatically by dotai sdd init. You can switch between tools mid-feature and the workflow continues without interruption.

Getting Started

# Install or upgrade dotai
npm install -g @nbslabs/dotai

# Initialize your project
dotai init

# Enable SDD
dotai sdd init

# Create your first feature
dotai sdd new my-feature

# Write your idea in .ai/sdd/my-feature/idea.md
# Then begin the workflow
/sdd-specify my-feature
/sdd-decompose my-feature
/sdd-plan my-feature
/sdd-implement my-feature
/sdd-evaluate my-feature
/sdd-review my-feature
/sdd-sync my-feature

Key Takeaways

  1. Structure beats intelligence. AI agents are capable enough. What they lack is a framework that channels their output toward your actual intent.
  2. Specification is the contract. Writing specs before code is not bureaucracy. It is the mechanism that aligns agent output with developer intent, eliminating the most expensive form of waste: building the wrong thing.
  3. Automated evaluation closes the loop. Without a verification step, you are trusting the agent's interpretation. With evaluation baked into the workflow, the spec is enforced, not merely referenced.
  4. Human review at the right moments. Four checkpoints, positioned before irreversible downstream work begins. No review fatigue, no wasted cycles.

The 8-phase workflow does not slow development down. It eliminates the rework that currently makes AI-assisted coding unpredictable. Your intent flows through specification, decomposition, planning, implementation, evaluation, review, and knowledge sync. Eight phases, zero ambiguity.
